tier_reason: Independent third-party suite rust-leipzig/regex-performance (src/onig.c, src/pcre2.c, src/cppstd.cpp, src/main.c) with public code, CMake flags and a named CPU (Threadripper 3960X) shows Oniguruma beating std::regex on all 15 shared patterns and the PCRE2 interpreter on 10 of 17, but the compiler is not named, so not A. Corroborated by the 2015 sljit regex_perf page (GCC 4.8.2 -O3, CPU without SKU), which shows the same per-pattern wins over interpreted PCRE2.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Mixed result, numbers in ms read from the repo's results_20221012.png (shown in the README). Versus PCRE2 interpreter ('pcre' column), Oniguruma is faster on 10 of the 17 patterns it can run: [a-z]shing 9.5 vs 432.9; [a-q][^u-z]{13}x 22.8 vs 417.5; .{0,2}(Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn) 48.8 vs 3201.7; .{2,4}(Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn) 48.2 vs 3330.2; \s[a-zA-Z]{0,12}ing\s 42.2 vs 314.9; ([A-Za-z]awyer|[A-Za-z]inn)\s 114.6 vs 755.5; [a-zA-Z]+ing 379.9 vs 837.3 (ratios 45.6x, 18.3x, 65.6x, 69.1x, 7.5x, 6.6x, 2.2x, derived from page data); the other three wins are near ties or small (\b\w+nn\b 436.6 vs 573.2, (?i)Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn 149.9 vs 227.5, Tom.{10,25}river|river.{10,25}Tom 42.6 vs 43.8). Versus PCRE2 JIT ('pcre-jit' column) it wins on only 4 of 17: [a-q][^u-z]{13}x 22.8 vs 114.8 (5.0x); .{0,2}(Tom|...) 48.8 vs 176.3 (3.6x); .{2,4}(Tom|...) 48.2 vs 166.7 (3.5x); \s[a-zA-Z]{0,12}ing\s 42.2 vs 59.7 (1.4x) (derived from page data). It is slower than the interpreter on 7 patterns, for example Twain 11.2 vs 2.5, ∞|✓ 21.1 vs 0.5 and (.*?,){13}z 5558.3 vs 567.5 (JIT 32.6). Versus std::regex ('cppstd' column) it is faster on all 15 patterns where both ran, from 2.2x ([a-zA-Z]+ing 379.9 vs 853.3) to 41.7x (.{2,4}(Tom|...) 48.2 vs 2010.4), e.g. [a-q][^u-z]{13}x 22.8 vs 726.3 (31.9x) and .{0,2}(Tom|...) 48.8 vs 1941.8 (39.8x) (ratios derived from page data); \p{Sm} is n/a for Oniguruma (ASCII encoding) and std::regex.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Harness (CMakeLists.txt at HEAD, the 2022-10-13 commit that produced the chart): default build type Release, -O3 plus -march=native -fsigned-char -fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables -fno-stack-protector and GCC-style warnings (-Wstack-usage=5000); CMAKE_C_FLAGS -std=c11 and CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS -std=c++11, while CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20 is also set, so the effective C++ standard flag is ambiguous. Compiler name and version not stated. Oniguruma and PCRE2 (PCRE2_SUPPORT_JIT=ON) are ExternalProject builds of upstream master (vendor/CMakeLists.txt) given only -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, so they use their own CMake Release flags (Oniguruma's CMakeLists sets none, so CMake's -O3 -DNDEBUG) and not -march=native; versions unpinned. std::regex is compiled into the harness with the harness flags.
corrections.caveats: Third-party community shootout, not a project claim: Oniguruma's own README and docs carry no benchmark. The numbers exist only as a PNG (results_20221012.png, October 2022 run), not as a data file, and were read from the image. The README says the tool prints the best time of 5 repeats but src/onig.c and pcre2.c fill a times array and report mean and standard deviation. Compiler is not named, tier A is therefore borderline; Oniguruma and PCRE2 versions are whatever master was in 2022. Match counts are printed but not asserted equal across engines, and Oniguruma runs in ASCII encoding while PCRE2 runs in default (non-UTF) mode with PCRE2_MULTILINE, so semantics are close but not identical. It loses to PCRE2 JIT on 13 of 17 patterns, so the win holds only against the interpreter, not against the usual fast PCRE2 configuration. Snippet-only, not opened (hosts blocked here): a 2003 mailing-list post by the author said Oniguruma was 10-20% faster than PCRE 3.9 under ASCII encoding (obsolete PCRE 3.x), and Heng Li's regex benchmark (onig-posix 5.9.2 vs PCRE 8.10 and RE2 2010) was summarised as onig fastest on '|'-free regexes; neither used PCRE2. Verifier additions: the chart is a single run; times are means of 5 repeats measured with clock() (process CPU time), and the repository HEAD (commit #19, 2022-10-13, 'updated the benchmarks') is the harness that produced the chart. The harness's -march=native applies only to the driver and the header-only std::regex code; Oniguruma and PCRE2 are ExternalProject builds that receive only -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, so they use their own CMake Release flags. The repo's Dockerfile uses Debian 9 g++, but the published run was on Ubuntu 20.04.5, so the Dockerfile does not identify the compiler. std::regex was built with std::regex::optimize (ECMAScript) and cannot run the (?i) rows; baseline_stdlib libstdc++ is inferred (Ubuntu toolchain, no -stdlib flag in the CMake files), not stated. Independent corroboration with an older pairing: Zoltan Herczeg's sljit regex_perf page (2015, Oniguruma 5.9.6 vs PCRE2 10.10, GCC 4.8.2 -O3, Intel Xeon 2.67GHz without SKU, harness regex-test.tgz) shows the same shape on x86-64 Linux: Oniguruma beats interpreted PCRE2 on 6 of 15 patterns ([a-z]shing 15 vs 564 ms, [a-q][^u-z]{13}x 61 vs 746, .{0,2}(Tom|...) 127 vs 5164, .{2,4}(Tom|...) 124 vs 5298, \s[a-zA-Z]{0,12}ing\s 78 vs 592, ([A-Za-z]awyer|[A-Za-z]inn)\s 243 vs 1112) and loses on the other 9, and beats PCRE2-JIT only on .{0,2}/.{2,4}(Tom|...) and \s[a-zA-Z]{0,12}ing\s (127 vs 443, 124 vs 487, 78 vs 140 ms). That page was written by the PCRE2-JIT author. Oniguruma has no JIT, is a backtracker (the (.*?,){13}z row is 5558.3 ms), and the repository was archived by its author on 2025-04-24.

notes: All numbers in claimed_speedup match the PNG (onig, pcre, pcre-jit, cppstd columns checked row by row; 10/17 vs interpreter, 4/17 vs JIT, 15/15 vs std::regex). Shortcomings to record: not faster than PCRE2-JIT (loses 13 of 17), mixed vs interpreted PCRE2, compiler unnamed, single 2022 run with unpinned master builds, archived 2025-04-24, catastrophic backtracking on (.*?,){13}z. Not a duplicate; Onigmo (fork) is not listed.
